content.title: About
content.content: Veal scallopini are thinly pounded pieces of veal quickly sautéed until golden. The dish is traditionally served with a lemon‑caper butter sauce. Veal is pale pink, tender, and has a mild flavor, making scallopini a staple in European cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “scallopini” comes from the Italian “scallopare,” meaning “to thinly slice.”
Veal contains less fat than beef, which makes it a leaner protein option.
Classic scallopini are finished with a butter‑lemon‑caper sauce, sometimes called “mélange.”
In Italy the dish is often paired with pasta, risotto, or a light vegetable side.
Veal scallopini are frequently used in fine‑dining menus as a base for more elaborate sauces.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Veal provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, veal has less saturated fat, supporting heart‑healthy eating patterns.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Mineral source
items.content: Veal contains zinc, iron, and phosphorus, supporting immunity, blood formation, and bone health.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The tender texture of veal makes it easier to digest than tougher cuts of beef.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef or veal.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Although leaner, veal still contains cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Foodborne pathogens
items.content: Undercooked veal can harbor bacteria such as Salmonella or E. coli.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions may cause heaviness in those with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve veal scallopini hot, typically drizzled with a lemon‑caper butter sauce. They can be added to salads, tossed with pasta, or used as a sandwich filling. Pair with light sides such as steamed vegetables or a green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw veal pieces in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. Cooked scallopini should be eaten within 24 hours, or stored in a sealed container in the fridge. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Reheat cooked scallopini to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.
